title: I Have $250,000 Left to Invest in Retirement. Here’s Where I Plan to Put It (and What I’m Avoiding).
summary: Dividing a retirement portfolio into short-, middle- and long-term horizons can help you assign each part to specific expenses.
body_markdown:
[Retirement investments](https://smartasset.com/retirement/safest-investments-for-retirees) generally fall into three groups: cash and short-term holdings covering expenses you will have to pay soon, bonds and other income sources for your middle years, and stocks for long-term growth. Here is an example with $250,000 to show where you may (and may not) invest your retirement money.


## Match Each Retirement Investment to a Timeline


Not every dollar in your[retirement portfolio](https://smartasset.com/retirement/best-investments-for-retirees) has the same job. Money you expect to use in the next few years should be easier to access and less exposed to market swings, while money you will not touch for a decade or more has more time to recover from market declines.


One way to organize this is to match different parts of your savings with a timeline for expected expenses. The table compares each time horizon with investments that fit that period, the expenses they aim to cover and the risks to consider:


Portion Time horizon Example holdings What it covers What it protects against Drawback


Near-term spending Next 1-3 years High-yield savings, CDs, Treasury ladder Living expenses, bills and planned purchases Having to sell investments during a market decline Returns often lag inflation, and CDs sometimes carry early-withdrawal penalties


Intermediate income Years 4-10 Treasurys, investment-grade bonds, bond funds Expenses not covered by Social Security, pensions or other income Relying too heavily on stocks for money used within several years Bond prices fall when interest rates go up, and corporate bonds carry credit risk


Long-term growth Year 11 and beyond Broad stock index funds Spending later in retirement, including higher future costs and healthcare Inflation and the risk of outliving your savings Stocks are vulnerable to sharp short-term losses, so this money should not be used for current expenses


The allocation depends on how much of your spending is already paid for by Social Security, pensions and other income. Retirees with a smaller gap often set aside less for near-term withdrawals, while those who depend more heavily on their portfolio typically keep a larger[cushion in cash and bonds.](https://smartasset.com/retirement/bucket-strategy-asset-allocations)


Cash and short-term investments are better suited for expenses that are due sooner, while stocks are generally more appropriate for money that can[stay invested through market declines](https://smartasset.com/retirement/experts-say-stay-invested-in-a-volatile-market-but-what-if-youre-approaching-retirement) . Using[long-term investments](https://smartasset.com/investing/investment-calculator) for current bills risks forcing sales at a bad time, while keeping too much long-term money in cash limits potential for growth.


The main risks come from taking too much or too little risk in the wrong part of the portfolio. Stocks sometimes fall sharply before near-term expenses are due, bonds lose value when interest rates go up and cash[loses purchasing power to inflation](https://smartasset.com/investing/inflation-calculator) . Higher-yield investments also bring additional credit or market risk to money that is supposed to remain stable.


**A** **[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_retirement_planning&utm_content=250000toinvestinretirementhereiswhereiamputtingit_a)** **can help test your retirement investment mix for different market conditions.**


## Where You Could Invest Your Retirement Money


A $250,000 portfolio does not have to produce all of your income from[interest and dividends](https://smartasset.com/investing/interest-income-vs-dividend-income) . Social Security, pensions and other income can cover part of your expenses, while the portfolio funds the rest through interest, dividends and planned withdrawals. The table shows how much annual income different parts of the portfolio could generate at example rates:


Timeline Amount Where the money could go Example rate or return Annual income or growth


Next 1-3 years $50,000 1-year United States Treasury 4.56% $50,000 × 4.56% = $2,280


Years 4-10 $100,000 5-year United States Treasury 4.65% $100,000 × 4.65% = $4,650


Year 11 and beyond $100,000 Broad stock index fund 7% illustrative return $100,000 × 7% = $7,000


In this example, $50,000 (20%) covers the next 1-3 years, $100,000 (40%) covers years 4-10 and the remaining $100,000 (40%) is for year 11 and beyond.


Assuming that each rate holds for those projected periods, the first part would earn $2,280 annually ($6,840 over three years), the second would give you $4,650 in one year ($32,550 in seven) and the third would grow by $140,000 in 20 years ($7,000 annually).


These amounts assume that each part stays invested the entire time, with no[compounding](https://smartasset.com/investing/what-is-compound-interest) or[reinvestment](https://smartasset.com/investing/should-i-reinvest-dividends) . The stock figure is the least certain of the three, since returns can swing widely from one year to the next.


[Treasury yields](https://smartasset.com/investing/treasury-yields) will change as securities mature and money is reinvested, so the bond portions could earn more or less than shown. Rates reflect market yields on November 25, 2026, and the 7% stock return is an example instead of a fixed return.1


## Where You May Want to Avoid Investing


With a $250,000 retirement portfolio, losses from concentration, high-risk income investments or poorly timed sales can take a bite out of your nest egg. The table shows four common mistakes, why they can hurt your savings and the red flags to look for:


Mistake Why It Can Backfire Warning Sign


Chasing the highest yield Higher yields often come with more credit, market or liquidity risk The yield is far above similar investments


Concentrating in one stock or sector A decline in one company or industry can hit a large share of the portfolio at once One holding makes up a large portion of the account


Keeping long-term money in cash Savings accounts and CDs can lose purchasing power to inflation over many years Money intended for later retirement remains mostly in cash


Selling after a market drop Selling turns a temporary decline into a realized loss and leaves less money invested for a recovery Withdrawals are coming from stocks immediately after a sharp decline


Using the example, if the $100,000 stock portion drops 30% in a market decline, that would be a $30,000 loss, and selling right after the drop would make it permanent. A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_retirement_planning&utm_content=250000toinvestinretirementhereiswhereiamputtingit_a) can help identify where too much of your retirement money is exposed to one type of risk.
